name: Hydroxycut

lead: Hydroxycut is a mainstream fat-burner brand launched in 2002 by MuscleTech and now sold by Iovate. People use it during cutting phases to feel more energised, curb appetite and get leaner alongside diet and exercise.

Formulas have changed from ephedra-era versions to current blends built on caffeine and robusta coffee extract (chlorogenic acids). The company cites two studies of its coffee extract, and critics have said independent evidence for the finished products is lacking.

paras: Taken as capsules or powders during a cut, usually with a calorie deficit and training, often before workouts for the energy boost. Users typically cycle it over a diet phase.

In 2009 the FDA warned consumers to stop using Hydroxycut products after reports of liver damage and at least one death, and the maker recalled them. Case series describe liver injury, and stimulant versions carry caffeine effects such as jitteriness and poor sleep.

angle.text: Hydroxycut is a mass-market caffeine fat burner that people use during cutting phases for energy and appetite control on the way to a leaner look. Current formulas centre on caffeine and robusta coffee extract; the evidence cited comes mostly from manufacturer-linked studies.

lead: Hydroxycut is a brand of over-the-counter weight-loss and fat-burner dietary supplements introduced in 2002 and developed by MuscleTech, a Toronto-area company whose assets were largely sold in 2003-2004 to Iovate Health Sciences, which continues to sell it. [1][2] Formulations have changed repeatedly: early versions contained ephedra, later ones included ingredients associated with liver injury, and current products are built around caffeine and plant extracts such as robusta coffee extract. [1][2]

On 1 May 2009 the US FDA warned consumers to stop using Hydroxycut products after reports of serious health problems including liver damage and at least one death, and the manufacturer issued a voluntary recall; reformulated products were later returned to market. [2] Case series in the medical literature describe liver injury associated with Hydroxycut. [3][4][5]

The company markets the products for adults combining them with diet and exercise and cites two human studies of its primary ingredient, while critics have said published evidence of effectiveness and safety for the final products is lacking. [1][2]

paras: Hydroxycut is sold as caplets, capsules, liquids and gummies, in stimulant and non-stimulant variants. [1] Current products centre on caffeine and Coffea canephora robusta extract standardised for chlorogenic acids, with variants adding yohimbe extract, apple cider vinegar, B vitamins or other botanicals; product pages describe the caffeine content of stimulant versions as comparable to about two cups of coffee. [1]

Before 2004 some formulations contained ephedra, which the FDA banned that year after 155 deaths were attributed to it, the first FDA ban of a dietary supplement. [2] Wikipedia states that pre-2009 formulations contained several substances with potential to harm the liver, including hydroxycitric acid, and that after 2009 caffeine was the only ingredient carried over. [2]

Hydroxycut launched in 2002. MuscleTech faced ephedra-related lawsuits from 2000, with about 80 pending by 2004, and a 2003 Missouri attorney general suit over "clinically proven" fat-burner claims that settled for $100,000. [2] MuscleTech filed for bankruptcy in June 2005, and Iovate continued the brand. Xiwang Foodstuffs acquired Iovate in 2016 in a deal reported at $730 million. [2]
By 2009 about 15 percent of Americans had tried weight-loss supplements and Hydroxycut was selling around a million units a year. [2]

The manufacturer cites two human studies of its robusta coffee extract reporting average weight losses of about 10.95 pounds over 60 days and 3.7 pounds over eight weeks. [1] A 2010 paper in the World Journal of Gastroenterology criticised two studies used in Hydroxycut marketing as small, short and lacking disclosure of manufacturer funding, and noted the company had not published long-term safety or efficacy studies of its final products. [2]

The FDA's May 2009 warning cited 23 reports of serious problems including liver damage, and said liver injury appeared relatively rare. [2] A 2010 case series in the American Journal of Gastroenterology adjudicated Hydroxycut-associated liver injury after the recall, and earlier reports in the Annals of Internal Medicine (2005) and World Journal of Gastroenterology (2008) described acute hepatitis in users. [3][4][5] Broader reviews of dietary-supplement hepatotoxicity include Hydroxycut among implicated products. [6][7]

Other reports include rhabdomyolysis, a 2010 case report of atrial fibrillation linked to the green tea extract in a discontinued version, and a 2013 case report of ulcerative colitis. [2] Product labels carry caffeine warnings. [1]
No forum threads were available for this entry. Hydroxycut appears in bodybuilding and cutting discussions as a mainstream fat-burner brand.

Published clinical evidence for Hydroxycut consists of the manufacturer-cited studies of its primary ingredient and a set of case series and case reports of adverse events, mainly liver injury. [1][3][4][5] No independent randomised trial of the finished products was identified in the sources reviewed.
